### TO THE READERS.

<meta>catchword: au-</meta>

In these last few years, such a great rumor regarding this Theology has spread everywhere that everyone—the unlearned and the learned alike—has wanted to know something about it; indeed, they have wanted to judge it and chatter about it, whether with good or ill intent. Among other things contributing to some knowledge of this subject, a small book (a) was published in the French language <note>original: "sermone Gallico"</note> containing three or four excellent treatises of a deeply Mystical nature. The first and most prominent of these was that famous *German Theology*, or *Teutonic* [Theology] <note>original: "Theologia Germanica, sive Teutonica"; a 14th-century mystical treatise that emphasized the imitation of Christ and the abandonment of the self</note>, nor were the remaining works of any less value. To these was prefixed a *Preface* which partly indicated the more general principles of **Mystical Theology**, and partly defended it from the censures of some of its adversaries. In this way, an opportunity was provided so that anyone possessed by a curiosity for this subject could know more certainly—rather than from common rumor—what that Mystical Theology truly was, which was so greatly discussed by everyone at that time, being praised by some and condemned by others. Since

Wetstein.* <note>original French: "La Theologie Réelle, vulgairement ditte la Theologie Germanique, avec quelques autres traités de même nature &c. Amsterd. 1700. chez H. Wetstein."</note>

However, since not all learned men were proficient in French <note>original: "Gallice scientes"</note>, excerpts were subsequently taken from that book. First, those things which had been said more generally in its preface concerning **Mystical Theology** were selected, while more specific points or those relating to controversial matters were left out. Next, the entire final part of that same book, the *Letter on the Characteristics of Mystics* <note>original: "Characteribus Mysticorum Epistola"</note>, was included. These are the very works which, as I mentioned at the start of this preface, were translated into Latin and published anonymously <note>literally "with the name suppressed"</note> under the title: *A Shorter Concept of Peaceful and Mystical Theology, and of its Authors; for the benefit of the Learned who desire a succinct and yet solid and fruitful exposition of Theological and Spiritual matters without extensive reading.* Indeed, as I advised in that same work, I am now restoring these pieces here, made more complete with annotations and additions, even within the **Catalogue** <note>original: "Catalogo"; likely referring to a list of mystical authors or works</note> itself.

I hope these will suffice for the purpose I have undertaken: namely, first, that those who wish to judge **Mystical Theology** <note>the study of direct, experiential union with the Divine</note> may draw from this work the knowledge required to judge it, at least in a general way, and from there draw—

### TO THE READERS.

—draw <note>original: "haurire"; this completes the sentence from the previous page</note> as much as is necessary; and so avoid that manner of acting—unworthy of a learned man, or even of the most humble layman—by which some, even among quite haughty theologians, have dared and still dare to pass judgment on that Theology with blind impulse. This they do despite being so unrefined and ignorant of the subject that they mistake an entirely different Theology—namely, **Allegorical** or **Symbolic** <note>theologies based on interpreting metaphors or outward signs rather than direct experience</note>—for **Mystical Theology**, much like taking a cloud for Juno <note>original: "nubem pro Junone"; a classical reference to the myth of Ixion, who was deceived by a cloud shaped like the goddess Juno, here meaning to mistake a phantom or surface-level image for the reality</note>.

Furthermore, as for the second and principal part of my proposal: if any should feel themselves in some way inclined toward this Theology, they may learn here where, or in which **Authors**, those things may be found which can be of help and benefit to anyone.

I do not promise a complete treatise on mystical matters; nor do I promise a History or a **universal Library** <term>Bibliothecam universalem; a comprehensive bibliography or catalog of all books on a subject</term> of these matters or of the **Mystical Authors** themselves. Instead, I offer a most general and brief demonstration or mention of the former; while of the latter—

# AUTHOR’S PREFACE

—certain <note>original: "versos" (likely "veros"); the author is continuing his description of the "latter" (the Authors) mentioned on the previous page</note> specific internal and principal **characteristics**, and sometimes a summary of the doctrine, and of the principles and method, or the manifold diversity of paths which various people use in different ways. These we have condensed into a few categories—and not very many at that—while indicating for each one the **Authors**, both from the more recent (and these indeed especially) as well as from the ancient ones. 

I have not included all of them, certainly, nor even as many as could have been; rather, I have selected from the most distinguished authors a no less distinguished portion—those who are most sufficient to serve as examples and means for our **purpose** <term>scopum; the target or end goal of a study</term>. Occasionally, these have been decorated here and there with certain historical details, which serve as ornaments no less useful than they are pleasant. 

The main **goal** <note>original: "Scopus"</note>, however, is this: since among the many readers eager for good and divine things, the constitution of the mind is not the same everywhere, nor is there the same kind of inclination, nor is the taste of the soul the same or even similar; therefore, each person may be able to see here—as if in a condensed and **SELECTED LIBRARY** <term>Bibliotheca Selecta; a curated collection of essential texts</term>—which—

-># TO THE READERS.<-

—for he <note>the reader</note> ought to choose from many writers, so that his own inclination and unique taste in this matter can be satisfied. Furthermore, if he is truly of a good soul, he might perhaps find an opportunity to attain certain remarkable and uniquely solid **rewards**, compared to which everything else in the world cannot but become completely worthless to him. # TO THE READERS.

—receive only the ideas or images of these things, or rather, they even manufacture them. I have shown that this is the faculty of human *Reason*, which for that reason, along with its acts and exercise, I have called *active*: but those [other faculties] are *passive*, as they do not produce their own objects or their living outpourings <note>original: *influvia*; see previous page note on the flow of divine energy</note>, but rather experience and receive them.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In relation to spiritual Objects, such passive faculties are a certain inward and even immense hunger or desire of the soul, and likewise the passive intellect <term>intellectus paſſivus; the capacity of the mind to receive truth directly from God rather than working it out through logic</term>, the eye of the spiritual soul (in which the seat of faith is). Furthermore, there are many more spiritual senses in the innermost parts of a person, which are fit to be affected by God, by divine things, and by their flowings-out <note>original: *effluentiis*</note> in a real, living, and solid way.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;By contrast, a soul affected only by the ideas of *Reason* is affected superficially, in a shadowy way, and in a manner that is dead, vanishing, and entirely like a mere painting; for the ideas themselves are only certain dead and sterile pictures, and utterly fleeting. Now, if anyone brings to the reading of mystical subjects <note>original: *rerum myſticarum*</note> only the ideal and shadowy faculty of their own *Reason*, and by reading through their active intellect—

# Author's Preface

—stirs up for itself, by its own industry, *ideas* that are as congruent as possible with the things it reads. It then joins, separates, and compares these ideas, drawing from them consequences—whether suitable or unsuitable—and amplifies them, reasoning about them more and more. Yet, if a person employs nothing else than his own human Reason <term>humanam Rationem; the logical, analytical mind as opposed to spiritual intuition</term> acting in this manner, he labors entirely in vain. 

Through this method, he will more often than not manufacture only empty fictions and absurd chimeras for himself, even from the most diligent reading of the Most Holy Scriptures <note>original: *Sanctiſſimorum ſcriptorum*; this refers to the Bible and perhaps the writings of the Church Fathers</note>. This occurs, of course, because of the immense depravity and corruption of our Reason. Consequently, it is inevitable that such a person will not only remain ignorant of divine realities <note>original: *res diviniores*</note>, but will even reject them. In the end, he becomes a shameless mocker and a singular adversary of these truths and their divine Authors. 

Indeed, even if this same person were able to form the most accurate ideas of all spiritual things <note>original: *spiritalium*</note> through his own reasoning—though this is, in fact, impossible—he would still achieve nothing but empty shadows and pictures that are utterly sterile and devoid of life. These are so far from [nourishing] his soul— <note>The text ends mid-word at *ani-*; the catchword *mam* on the next page completes *animam*, or "soul."</note>

# AUTHOR'S PREFACE

These seekers, however, because they are still weak and of a coarser understanding, employ at the same time—as a kind of support—not only certain external things, but also the ideas and diligence of their own **Reason** <note>original: *Rationis*</note>. They do this by occupying that Reason as much as possible with **spiritual objects** <note>original: *spiritualia objecta*</note> to be represented to themselves conceptually, while simultaneously adding prayers of sincere desire toward God. They do this so that He might kindly bestow reality itself, along with His divine outpourings and lights, not only upon Reason, but also upon the heart, the **passive intellect** <term>intellectui passivo; the receptive capacity of the soul that stops its own thinking to wait for God's direct illumination</term>, and all our innermost depths.

In this exercise, where both the "real" and the "shadowy" faculties <note>The "real" faculties are the heart and soul; "shadowy" refers to the intellect or reason which only sees reflections of the truth</note> are used together, a danger arises. If they conduct themselves in such a way that they give the greater portion to Reason—exercising it more through **logical arguments** <note>original: *ratiocinia*</note> about ideas than by ardently and frequently offering up the heart, the intellect, the desires, and all that is within to God and His operations—then they will either make no progress at all, or, as the conceptual and active faculty finally gains the upper hand, they will degenerate into thinkers who are merely conceptual, superficial, proud, and false, and—

# TO THE READERS.

** 3

...deceived spiritual and mystical people, even though they previously possessed certain truly solid and real experiences. Because of those past experiences, they still appear to themselves to be most "solid" <note>In this context, "solid" refers to being spiritually grounded or possessing authentic substance</note>, and they often most boldly and confidently judge and condemn others who are not like them—even those who are, in truth, most solid. In fact, hardly any other danger or type of deception can occur that is greater than this. 

But if they would instead exercise themselves more and more in employing their real faculties and offering them to God, rather than in scrutinizing and debating ideas of divine things through the activity of their own **Reason**; and if, day by day, they would occupy themselves less and less with examining and weighing those ideas—including their various parts, cases, and difficulties—through logical arguments, they would find a better way. They should use the principal truths represented to them as an occasion to lift up to God that solid and sincere **depth of the Mind** <term>fundum Mentis; a mystical term referring to the "ground" or the deepest, most essential part of the soul where it meets the Divine</term> and of their real and innermost faculties (which Peter calls the **pure mind** <note>original Greek: *τὴν εἰλικρινῆ διάνοιαν* (tēn eilikrinē dianoian); 2 Peter 3:1</note>).

*Innumerable are they,* <term>Christian Reader<note>original: "Christiane Lector"; a standard formal address used by early modern authors to engage their audience.</note></term>*, who have written concerning* <term>Absolute Theology<note>original: "Theologia absoluta"; this refers to the study of divine truths as a fixed, complete system of dogmas or doctrines.</note></term>*, and that with no great benefit; but as for who might have written concerning* <term>Comparative Theology<note>original: "Theologia Comparativa"; in this historical context, it refers to the study of how different Christian doctrines and duties relate to one another in terms of their importance and practical application.</note></term>*, I have so far found no one.*

*the knowledge of God and the obedience rendered to His commands are more pleasing to God than sacrifices and burnt offerings,* <note>original: "Dei notitiam, & obsequium ipsius mandatis præstitum, magis Deo grata esse, quam sacrificia & holocausta"</note> 1 Samuel 15:22; Hosea 6:6. From this consideration flows the distinction of *skill, doctrine, or knowledge* concerned with religion, which can be called *Theological doctrine or knowledge*; this is divided into *Absolute* and *Respective, or Comparative*. *Absolute Theological Knowledge* considers its object insofar as it is revealed, prescribed, or instituted by God; it investigates those things proposed to us in the Word of God to be believed or done, and distinguishes them from other things. *Comparative Knowledge* of things pertaining to Religion—whether they be dogmas, precepts, or sacred rites—weighs their importance and significance. It observes the order in which they relate to one another; it teaches how to discern and distinguish accessories from principal matters, circumstantial things from substantial ones, and finally, the means from the ends.

Rather, it is likely that **God**, having already observed in man a certain distant and beginning disposition toward the love of created things, forbade him the use of that one tree for a specific reason: either because man’s affection was leaning toward it more than was right, or to warn man by this symbol that he possessed the rest of the things permitted to him only by the right of stewardship <note>original: "clientelae jure" — a legal concept where one holds property or rights under the protection and authority of a superior patron.</note>, maintaining a **Dependence on God** as the supreme Lord of all, to whom, for that very reason, he owed his highest love.

**Section 27.** If anyone should ask whether God could not have immediately reintegrated fallen man, and, once restored, confirmed him in **Grace** and **Holiness**, and placed him beyond all danger of falling, so that he would be no more liable to sin than the glorious **Angels**? I answer that a *confirmed state of grace and Holiness* is both the fruit and the reward of a constancy and firmness in the love of God that has been previously exercised and proven. By no other law was this state granted to the **Angels** who persisted in their duty and faithfulness, nor would it have been granted to **Adam**, except after a suitable period of probation <note>A period of testing or trial to prove one's character.</note> in the love of God had been faithfully completed. # ...or Comparative [Theology].

From this Schematic of Comparative Theology, it appears clearly that **Ecclesiastical Government** <term>Regimen Ecclesiasticum: the systems of leadership, hierarchy, and law that govern a church body</term> is merely a means for recovering the **love of the Divine** <note>original: *Numinis amorem*; "Numen" refers to the divine will or the presence of God</note>. In these disputes, seditions and riots are stirred up, and hatreds and enmities are practiced, to the great disgrace of the Christian name, the scandal of the weak, and the heavy decline—or should I say the ruin?—of **true piety**.

How much better it would be, and how much more conducive and well-advised for the honor of the Christian name, for piety, and for peace, if Christian men were to practice **mutual tolerance** here. # Theologia Pacifica,
## or Peaceable Theology

...neglecting the truth. Most Christians are found guilty of this fault: they value "correct faith" and personal conviction regarding non-essential matters more than the holiness of life—that holiness without which "no one will see the Lord" (Hebrews 12:14). 

By "non-essential," I mean almost all those dogmas <term>Dogmas: specific doctrines or articles of faith held by a particular church</term> that are unique to each individual Christian sect. This also includes certain sacred rites used in external worship, and particular forms of government regarding church polity <term>Polity: the internal organized structure and administration of a church</term>. These are matters about which a person may hold one opinion or another without any danger to their eternal salvation. 

Yet, people are less concerned with holiness than with these dogmas, both in themselves and in others. In their own personal practice, they devote themselves more to "purity" of orthodoxy <term>Orthodoxy: adherence to the "correct" or standard version of a belief system</term> and outward religious ceremonies than they do to humility, charity, the mortification of the flesh <term>Mortification of the flesh: the spiritual discipline of subduing worldly or physical desires</term>, or self-denial. 

Consequently, they welcome into their communion with open arms anyone who agrees with them in faith and outward worship, even if those people lead worldly and earthly lives. However, they exclude and turn away those who disagree with them as if they were strangers, even if those people are living pious and Christian lives. In this way, they are more occupied with winning disciples for their own particular sect than for Christ. Even if these converts do not become worse (like the proselytes of the Pharisees <note>original: *proselytis Pharisæorum*; a reference to Matthew 23:15, where Jesus warns that converts to legalistic sects can become more radical than their teachers</note>), they still gain nothing by simply moving from one camp to another...

### General Concept ###

This state is of great breadth, as is the diverse makeup of souls and the ways in which they must be cultivated. 

The modes and degrees of ***suspension*** are likewise very numerous; so much so that at times, in a certain person <note>original: "subjecto"</note>, almost no suspension presents itself; at other times, there is more; here very much, elsewhere still more. At certain times or in certain people, the suspensions may be absolute and perfect, and yet afterwards, there may be none at all in those passive minds <note>original: "mentibus paſſivis"</note>, which will be the most perfect of all. Since this can only be achieved through the power of the **Lord’s Spirit**—as the same **Holy Scripture** testifies—Man cast himself and all his descendants headlong into destruction when he attempted to bring help to himself by his own powers of mind and will, and tried to make himself perfect by his own methods.

Furthermore, through this separation—by which Man, torn away from God, wished to cling to himself and to the creatures subject to him—he was overwhelmed by darkness, vices, and corruption; thus, he became entirely alienated from his supreme purpose.

From this quagmire <note>original: *lerna*; literally referring to the swamp of the Hydra, used here to describe a vast and tangled "sea of evils."</note> of evils, he can only be rescued by the help of the **Divine Power** <note>original: *Divini Numinis*; referring to the divine will or the Godhead.</note> alone. In this way, that most noble work of God—which is Man himself, though lost through the **Fall** <note>original: *lapsu*; the theological concept of the Fall of Adam.</note> and plunged into an abyss of miseries—can be restored to wholeness.

And to accomplish this, **Supreme Goodness** offers itself to Man along with its **Divine Workings**; it is then for Man to consent to the Lord who is at work, and to accept the **Grace** offered,

The character of this enlightened author is, in my judgment, as follows: He urges, naturally, that the soul—through the <term>mortification</term> <note>the spiritual practice of "dying" to one's selfish impulses and vices</note> of its passions and vices, through the practice of virtues, and through the abandonment and denial of itself, its desires, its own will, self-love, and indeed all its own activity and all created things—should return to its **innermost depth** <note>original: *intimum suum fundum*; a central concept in Rhineland mysticism referring to the "ground of the soul" where the human meets the Divine</note>. It is there that the soul seeks and finally finds God, who reveals Himself in that very place through the **birth of His Divine Word** and through the breath of His **Holy Spirit**. He teaches that the soul should then preserve itself in this interior state through constant and lasting <term>introversion</term> <note>the act of turning one's focus inward toward God rather than outward toward the world</note>, so that God may be able to carry out His own will, His wonders, and His special ways of governance within it. However, this Teacher discusses these matters only in a general sense.

These begin first as active states and then become passive <note>In mystical theology, "active" states involve the soul's effort in prayer and virtue, while "passive" states are those where the soul is acted upon directly by God.</note>, occurring first in the lower faculties of the soul and afterwards in the higher ones—the memory, the intellect, and the will. This system of **Mystical Theology** is as excellent, as essential, as consummate, and as profound as any that has ever appeared.

### II. HENRY HERP <note>Latin: Henricus Harphius (c. 1410–1477), a Franciscan mystic whose "Theologia Mystica" had a profound influence on later Catholic spirituality.</note>

<margin>§. 8.</margin>
(8.) This author, whom I just now added to the number of those endowed with the character of Tauler, deserves an entirely special article. He is in excellent agreement with Tauler; yet he maintains a more exact method, touches more upon specific details, and proceeds far deeper: indeed, it must be admitted that before him—and perhaps even after him—no one has as successfully penetrated the internal states and their depth in a soul devoted to God as he has. This system of Mystical Theology <note>original: "Theologiæ Mysticæ"</note> is as excellent, as essential, as complete and profound, as has ever appeared.

<header>Letter. §. 10.</header>

Truly, **JOHN OF THE CROSS** belongs to the same rank as Harphius; indeed, he surpasses him significantly in those matters which are characteristic of this path. His aim is to elevate the purity of the Soul, providing us with a glimpse of the most sweet communion between the Supreme Majesty and a purified Soul. Beyond the Active Way of purification—which he describes using a method perfectly suited for refining the minds of learned seekers aspiring to the Heavens—and that same purification as it is achieved through the practice of Virtues (where he insists that one must always embrace both the most humble and the most difficult paths), the unique characteristic of John of the Cross is (1.) a universal nakedness <note>original: *nuditas*; referring to the spiritual "stripping" or detachment of the soul from all created things</note> of the Soul and its faculties. This stripping extends so far that it even pulls back all affection from all the sensible and special gifts of Divine Grace, which the Highest Goodness frequently grants to beginners <note>original: *tyronibus*; literally "recruits" or "novices"</note> in the spiritual school, whether these gifts flow through the channels of the senses, the imagination, or other mental faculties. He makes an exception only for the "substantial words" and "touches" of God <note>These refer to direct, intellectual communications from God to the essence of the soul that do not rely on physical images or emotional feelings</note>. Above all other authors, he particularly fortifies the Soul against every kind of spiritual illusion, no matter how they may appear; so much so...

He reduced everything to the single **Principle of the Will of God**, which expresses the very character of his books. This Principle, which is in no way controversial and is approved by the consensus of all Christians—and indeed by anyone who makes use of reason—contributes greatly to ensuring that all things are put into actual practice. It also serves to free those from error who imagine for themselves, or wish to persuade others, that the **spiritual life** <note>original: "Vitam spiritualem"</note> consists only in certain abstract and dry contemplations of an idle mind that is quiet and without action. 

**Canfield** <note>Referring to Benedict of Canfield, the English Capuchin mystic</note> insists that the **Will of God** alone should be the principle and the goal which one must look to in all things. Alluding to the Apostolic text of Romans 12, verse 2, he proposes that this will is threefold: namely, the **external and good**; the **internal and well-pleasing**; and finally the **intimate or essential**, which is supereminent and perfect. 

In the first part of his book, he explains how the **Will of God**—the rule of our actions—must be carried out or accepted. ### Of Mystic Authors,

# Letter. Section 53.

Christ was raised by His Father for the full completion <note>original: "consummationem"; implying the ultimate fulfillment or bringing to perfection.</note> of all things. John 17:21, 23.

<margin>Section 53.</margin>
(53.) So that the solid, spiritual, and lofty doctrine of this Author may be made clearer, it is necessary to establish and carefully weigh the theses or principles that follow.

I. Spiritual and internal things are the origin, reality, force, and power of all things. For truly all things, and especially bodily things, *were nothing; and, by the testimony of Holy Scripture itself (Hebrews 11:3),* they began to exist only through the power of spiritual and invisible things, of which those [bodily things] are like outgrowths, and, if I may put it this way, like shoots <note>original: "stolones"; botanical term for runners or suckers of a plant.</note> or visible manifestations of the state and powers that reside within invisible things.

II. Therefore, just as internal things are disposed, in that same way external and material things will behave; because these proceed from those, and as the cause is, so is the effect.

III. If therefore the spiritual thing—namely the soul <note>original: "anima"</note>—and all its internal acts are well-disposed, consequently its external and bodily aspect will undoubtedly be correctly ordered.

### Letter. Section 55.

Furthermore, opinions, persuasions, theories, speculations, ideas, and discourses are by no means *life and spirit*:

Since all these things do not constitute the *one-essential life* <note>original: "vitam uni-reälem"; Hiel’s term for a state where the soul is fundamentally merged with divine reality.</note> *or true life in divine unity and simplicity*, they cannot be the direct and living means for the restoration either of any individual person, or of the entire Universe in general:

1. Therefore, to cling to these things as if they were the direct and living means is hypocrisy, Pharisaism <note>Refers to the religious attitude of focusing on external rules and intellectual pride rather than internal spiritual transformation.</note>, self-righteousness, one’s own holiness or a holiness of one’s own choosing—an imaginary and carnal holiness. Thus the Author expresses his mind in many places, and for this reason he strongly rebukes the Christians of these latter times.

2. To cling to these things as if they were the end or goal toward which one must strive and in which one must find rest is to build gods and idols from them. It is idolatry before God according to the same Author, who demonstrates that the Christianity of this age is already far too infected by this barely noticed idolatry.

3. But to use these things (as much as possible) as accessories and as coarse or elementary means to advance oneself toward the *real life in divine unity*, pe- <note>The text breaks off here; the catchword suggests the word may be related to "peculiar" or "properly" (Latin: *peculiare*).</note>

<margin>Section 57.</margin> (57.) This Author lived about one hundred and fifty years ago. He was a layman and unlearned, knowing no language except Dutch <note>original: "Belgicam"; refers to the Low German/Dutch dialects of the Netherlands.</note>, which he himself professes in his books to be his mother tongue. On this point there is no reason to doubt, even though in his allegorical explanations of Scripture, he always renders the proper names of the Bible—both Hebrew and Greek—by providing an interpretation that exactly corresponds to their etymologies <note>the study of the origin and original meaning of words.</note>. He was able to accomplish this because he was an intimate friend of the famous and learned Arias Montanus <note>Benito Arias Montano (1527–1598), a Spanish orientalist and editor of the Antwerp Polyglot Bible.</note>, who translated everything for him. Montanus held him in such high regard that he declared in a public testimony that the man was a *witness of the living Christian truth* <note>original: "Christianæ veritatis viventis testem"</note>, upon whom the very power and truth of Christ bestowed the name **HIEL**. Specifically, the word *Hiel* denotes *the life of God* <note>original: "vitam Dei"; from the Hebrew 'Chay' (life) and 'El' (God).</note>. He was also an associate of the famous printer Plantin <note>Christophe Plantin (c. 1520–1589), one of the most influential publishers of the Renaissance.</note>, who printed all of his books in Dutch and French with tireless devotion, and with that elegance and beauty which this skilled printer was accustomed to achieve in his work. However, Plantin did not put his own name on them, nor the date or place of printing, undoubtedly because of the fear of *the Jews* <note>original: "Judæorum"; in this mystical context, it likely refers to legalistic religious authorities or the Spanish Inquisition, whom the group viewed as modern-day Pharisees.</note>, and fearing lest he might stir up troublesome disturbances for himself.

(61.) **HERMANN HERBERTS**, a preacher of the Reformed at Gouda <note>A Dutch city known for its more tolerant religious atmosphere during the Reformation.</note> more than a century ago, abundantly expresses the mind and character of our Author <note>The "Anonymous Author" referred to here and on previous pages is likely the mystic David Joris.</note> in a distinguished Dutch treatise which he published in the year 1584, titled: *A Brief Exposition of the Words of Saint Paul, Romans 2:28: For he is not a Jew, who is one outwardly, etc.* This treatise is a sort of system of **positive theology** <term>positive theology: A branch of theology based on specific revealed truths and historical facts rather than purely philosophical or rational speculation.</term>—by the leave of **Voetius** <note>Gisbertus Voetius (1589–1676), a Dutch Calvinist theologian known for his rigid orthodoxy; the author here politely acknowledges Voetius's influential bibliography.</note> in his *Library for the Student of Theology*—most solid and useful, and of which he made a notable Defense in the year 1591. The writings of our **Anonymous Author** had been of great benefit to him; indeed, as it is reported, he himself had promoted the publication and republication of many of those works.

(62.) Among the ancients, **SAINT EPHREM** appears with the same character. He was a Syrian by nation and a Deacon of Edessa in the fourth century; a man whom the entire Christian Church has never ceased to both venerate and admire, and of whom **Chrysostom** <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), a prominent Early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople known for his eloquent preaching.</note> says:

> (a) *Where is that great Syrian Ephrem, the awakener of the sluggish; the discipline, instructor, and exhorter of the young; the mirror of Monks; the leader of those doing penance; the sword and spear against heretics; the vessel of virtues, and the dwelling place and lodging of the Holy Spirit?* <note>original: "Ubi Syrus ille Ephrem magnus, obtorpeſcentium excitator; juvenum disciplina, instructor, atque exhortator; Monachorum ſpeculum; dux pænitentium; framea ac ſpiculum adverſus hæreticos; virtutum receptaculum, & Spiritus Sancti habitaculum atque diverſorium?"</note>

That saint was (just like our **Anonymous Author**) unlettered and unlearned; nevertheless, the **Holy Spirit** <note>original: "Spiritus S."</note> had instilled into his mind and heart the substance, nay, even the very words of all the **Holy Scripture** <note>original: "Scripturæ S."</note>, and had granted him a tongue which both explained the same and impressed it upon the hearts of others with such efficacy as no eloquence, whether natural or cultivated by study, could reach. This is most clearly demonstrated by his divine works, which in truth are nothing but a weaving together of the substance and terms of the **Holy Bible** <term>Sacri Codicis: literally "The Sacred Codex," a common term for the Bible.</term>, aiming to recall the spirit of contrition into souls, to most severely lead mortals away from evil, and to strongly impel them toward good through every kind of inducement of fear, hope, and love that one can comprehend in the mind. His works were held in such high esteem that they were read publicly in the **Eastern Churches**. There exists a **Latin Version** of them which has several times been revised <note>original: "sub incudem revocata," an idiom meaning "brought back to the anvil" for refinement.</note>, and most recently in the year 1675 at Cologne. His *Testament*, along with certain of his short works, previously appeared in the old French dialect; but a new translation of it was provided by **Father Lallemant**, Chancellor of the University of Pari- <note>likely "Parisian," completed on the following page.</note>

(63.) Another of the ancients imbued with the same spirit and character was that great and divine <term>Saint Macarius the Egyptian</term> <note>Also known as Macarius the Great (c. 300–391 AD), a desert hermit whose spiritual writings were highly influential in mystical theology.</note>, a contemporary of Saint Ephrem, a hermit and a disciple of Saint Anthony; although he was unlearned, he was nevertheless powerful in miracles, in virtues, and in words. It is most clearly felt that the Spirit of the Supreme Deity <note>original: "Summi Numinis"</note> reveals therein the incredible misery and captivity of man under sin and the Demon; it reveals the means of emerging from that state through Christ and of reviving in his Spirit, who afterwards rules victorious souls and [performs] operations within them...

These are the principles upon which this holy Virgin everywhere relies, and which she inculcates and extends with living ardor and her whole heart. Found within this book are many distinguished Truths and not a few principles of great importance concerning the depth and faculties of the soul, the presence of God, and His operations, etc.

(65.) *The Evangelical Pearl* <note>original: "Margarita Evangelica"</note> has frequently been "brought back to the anvil" <note>a Latin idiom meaning to revise, refine, or reprint a work</note> in the French, Latin, German, and Dutch <note>original: "Belgica," referring here to the Dutch or Flemish vernacular</note> languages. They fashioned it according to the Latin edition from Cologne of the year 1545, which nonetheless is not the true original, but a translation by **Eschius** <note>Nicolaus van Esch (1507–1578), a Dutch priest and mystical writer</note>, in which the order was changed, and its three parts were restructured into four.

However, the greatest variation of all consists in this: for fear that the "wise ones of this world" might be offended by the revelation of whose pen produced this book—namely, a Virgin’s—they not only omitted the first preface, but also changed feminine terms into masculine ones toward the end. In that section, the first Dutch editor (who is believed to be the same Eschius) acknowledges that his conversion to God was achieved through the help of this Virgin, whom he calls the *Bride, Handmaid, and Friend of God* <note>original: "Dei Sponsam, Ancillam & Amicam"</note>. (70.) Among the anonymous short works is also the *German Theology* <note>original: "Theologia Germanica"; a 14th-century mystical treatise highly influential during the Reformation</note>, an ancient, famous, deeply radical, and most exquisite little book, which contains almost nothing but the pure principles of a most inward and practical Christian Theology. That God is everything, that man is nothing, the evil of self-appropriation <note>the tendency to claim for oneself what belongs to God</note>, the denial of oneself and of all other things; then the distinction between the true and false light, true and false freedom, and pure versus mercenary love <note>referring to love for God's sake versus love motivated by reward</note>—these constitute the argument treated therein. It is written indeed without a notable academic method, yet in such a way that it is felt to have proceeded from an inward solidity and from a soul illuminated by God. This little book was written in German by a Teutonic Knight <note>original: "Equite Teutonico"; an anonymous member of the Teutonic Order in Frankfurt</note>, and was edited in that language with great praise by [Martin] Luther, [Johann] Arndt, and others. It was later translated into Dutch and printed in Antwerp by the Plantin Press <note>one of the most famous printing houses in early modern Europe</note> with the approval of the Censor Silvestro Pardo in 1590. ### Letter. §. 81.

...with sincerity and simplicity, namely by referring all our actions to Him: both internal actions—that is, acts of adoration, blessing, praise, prayer, and a grateful heart—and external ones. These external actions are performed either through deeds, by doing everything in the company of God and according to His will, with order and tranquility, and offering all things to Him; or through words and conversation, by speaking to Him, albeit silently and without noise, at all times and on the occasion of any subject, whether pleasant <margin>§. 82.</margin> or unpleasant, good or evil. We should give thanks to Him for the former, while for the latter we should seek either help or forgiveness, praising Him for all things. Indeed, one should occasionally and for a moment interrupt their occupations for this purpose, in order to acquire a habit in this holy exercise. This practice, like a perpetual and sacred fire, will gradually consume all our defects and provide us the strength to crush the head of the serpent <note>A traditional biblical allusion to Genesis 3:15, representing the soul's victory over temptation or the devil through divine grace</note> on every occasion.

# On Mystic Authors

Her spiritual writings, written in French, have been released to the public. Her *Life* <note>original: *Vita*; her biography, often a requirement for the beatification process or as a model for other religious</note>, published separately in Antwerp in the year 1659, contains many details of no small importance regarding the way the Supreme Deity <note>original: *Summi Numinis*; a classical Latin way of referring to God</note> acts toward souls devoted to Him. In her *Works*, which were published together in Tournai in the year 1665, the truths and practice of Christian, interior, and mystical matters are treated with no less solidity and clarity than in the writings of those who are considered the leaders of the learned.

A more extensive treatise among these Works, titled *The Ruin of Self-Love* <note>original: *Ruina Amoris proprii*; "self-love" in this context refers to egoism or pride that hinders spiritual progress</note> (printed separately in Paris), explains the entire interior life in an orderly fashion. It depicts the states of that life through the metaphor <note>original: *emblema*; a symbolic representation or allegory</note> of the things that occur successively during the four seasons of the year, much as Ruysbroeck <note>Jan van Ruysbroeck (1293–1381), an influential Flemish mystic known as "the Divine Doctor"</note> did in his *The Adornment of the Spiritual Marriage* <note>original: *Ornatu nuptiarum spiritualium*</note>.

This work is divided into four books. In the *first*, she uncovers the hiding places and deceits of self-love and generally recounts the power of Divine Grace in destroying them. In the *second* book, she describes the increase of God’s grace in those who are making progress on the Way of Salvation, citing many passages from the *Song of Solomon* <note>original: *Cantico Salomonis*; traditionally interpreted by mystics as an allegory for the soul's relationship with God</note>. In the *third* book, she sets before our eyes the rigorous privations, temptations, and spiritual trials...

<header>Letter. §. 89.</header>

...our author <note>original: "illum nostrum"; referring to Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), the author of the *Historical and Critical Dictionary*.</note> by no means deserves trust in this kind of argument. Truly, it is evident that he wishes to proceed as if by logical proofs; yet it is no less evident that he perfectly masters the <term>shrewd practice of old foxes|original: "praxin veteratorum"; a term for the manipulative tactics used by seasoned or deceptive polemicists</term>, such as he has recognized elsewhere in certain unfaithful historians. These are men who, snatching up some raw historical fact, know how to season it as they go through a thousand tricks of fraud at their fingertips. They give it whatever flavor and color they please—whether sweet or bitter, white or black—depending on the changing impulses of their minds.

I discovered many passages in the works marked with a small line in the margin; if you look at these in isolation, they cannot help but make Bourignon's doctrine appear highly suspicious, often even blasphemous. However, if you join them to the preceding or following text, they have an excellent and pious meaning. (96.) The character of **Boehme** <note>Jacob Böhme (1575–1624), a German Lutheran mystic whose works, such as *The Signature of All Things*, explored the deep spiritual structures of the natural and divine worlds.</note>, who scrutinized the nature of things spiritual and physical, divine, angelic, human, and natural—should he be suspect to us, when a saying of **St. Paul** offers itself in total agreement with him?

> "No human eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the mind of man, what things God has prepared for those who love him. But God has revealed them to us through His Spirit. ### On Mystic Authors ###

...concerning what anyone might suggest here: either that I have omitted quite a few **Authors** of this class <note>original: *hujusce classis*</note>, of whom no mention was made; or, that I have brought forward too many; and that this profuse heap <note>original: *profusa hæc congeries*</note> cannot help but confuse those who, desiring to read the **Mystics**, will be uncertain which of them are to be selected, perhaps thinking that for this reason the reading of all of them is required. 

I confess, regarding the first point, that one might suggest this not without cause, being well aware of how many of them I have passed over; nevertheless, it seems to me that since I have mentioned a hundred and more, so many suffice for my purpose, which by no means required a greater number—indeed, not even this many. 

Regarding the second point, I am so far from declaring that the reading of all these **Authors** is necessary for those who aspire to a more solid **spiritual knowledge** <term>spiritualis cognitio: a deep, internal understanding of divine truths gained through experience rather than just academic study</term>; that, on the contrary, I recommend very few of them and a quite moderate reading, provided that one takes the opportunity from there to **descend into oneself** <note>original: *in se ipsum descendendi*; a key mystical practice of looking inward to find God</note>, and does not become preoccupied with dead ideas drawn from there through mere **speculation** <term>speculatio: theoretical or abstract thinking that lacks practical application or heart-felt conviction</term>; but rather implores the light and power of the **Divine Presence** <note>original: *Divini Numinis*</note>, so that to [him] the light...

# On the Authors of Mystical Letters. Section 100. #

...*Constantine de Barbançon* <note>original: *Constantinum de Barbançon*; a 17th-century Capuchin mystic known for his work "The Secret Paths of Divine Love"</note>, *Canfield* <note>Benet of Canfield, an influential English Capuchin</note>, and *Gelenius*. For living practice, look to the *Lives of the Fathers* <note>original: *Vitas Patrum*; a collection of the lives and sayings of the desert saints</note>, and especially *Saint Macarius* <note>Macarius the Great, an Egyptian monk whose "Spiritual Homilies" were highly influential in mystical circles</note>. These would be sufficient, in my judgment, for your purpose; however, those who wish to collect more will easily be able to satisfy their desire once they have read this letter of mine, which I could not end more fittingly than with a serious recommendation of the book called *The German Theology*:

<margin>(a) German Theology, chapter 9.</margin>
> (a) Although it is good to inquire or explore, and even to know, what good and holy men did (or wrote) or suffered, or how they lived, or what God worked (or produced) and willed in them and through them; nevertheless, it would be a hundred times better if a person explored and knew who and of what sort the state of their own life is, and what God is, wills, and does in them, and for what purpose God wishes to use them, or not. Therefore, this too is true, which is said: *NEVER IS IT SO GOOD TO GO OUT, BUT THAT TO REMAIN WITHIN IS BETTER.* <note>original: *NUNQUAM TAM BONUM EST EXIRE, QUIN SIT INTUS MANERE MELIUS*; a common theme in mystical literature emphasizing interiority over external curiosity.</note>

Behold to what end all truly spiritual books call us; if we act otherwise, we pursue their very substance with hatred.

<header>To the Letter on the Authority of Mystical Theology <note>original: *Ad Epist. de Auct. Myst.*</note>, Section 16.</header>

The core of his argument <note>original: *summa*; the "sum" or essence of the author's point.</note> returns to this: that a soul dedicated to purity of life and humility of spirit, and joining its affections to God, is illuminated by a ray of His wisdom. From this state, the soul knows God better and loves Him more excellently, tasting Him more sweetly after having yearned for Him more ardently; at last, it is touched by the Holy Spirit. In this most sublime and ineffable touch <note>original: *tactu*; "touch" is a technical term in mystical theology referring to a direct, non-conceptual experience of God's presence.</note>, the soul is finally granted a unique and intimate knowledge and contemplation of God, along with the purest love and an unspeakable taste and enjoyment. Indeed, in this matter, this author establishes the very substance—even the very peak—of **Mystical Theology** <note>The study of the soul's direct, experiential union with the Divine.</note>, and he insists upon it especially, setting aside those things that pertain to the purification of the soul, which are among the preparatory steps and are to be sought from other authors.

# Annotations & Additions

...having been written and then printed in Paris in the year 1683 by fertile presses. Otherwise, I would have had no hesitation in joining her to Saint Catherine of Genoa <note>original: *S. Catharinæ Genuensi*; a 15th-century Italian mystic known for her intense experiences of divine love and her service to the sick.</note> as a true companion, since she was governed by the same principle of divine and burning Love of God, and was consequently imbued with that same admirable and sacred *Character* as she. Indeed, it can even be asserted that her life and each of her ways of acting are something that, if not more admirable, is certainly more imitable, and therefore of more general usefulness for anyone. Among all the lives of holy souls that I have happened to read, I have never seen anything that is more admirable, solid, and sublime all at once.

The *Admirability* lies in this: that if there is anything of wonderful virtues, lights, and graces in what is most holy and divine in Christianity, all of it was found in a poor countrywoman, simple and illiterate <note>original: *idiota atque ἀναλφαβήτῳ*; the Greek term refers to one who cannot read or write, emphasizing her lack of formal theological training.</note>, who for as long as she lived always played the part of a maidservant.

The *Solidity* consists in the fact that everything in her flowed from the living Spirit of Christ dwelling within, and was founded on union with Him through living charity; and these things were not only imitable, but were also such that they can be reconciled with the actions of life, even external ones.

Finally, the *Sublimity* here was such that, whether in the highest degree of the Christian spirit, or in the most sublime things of which the *Mystics* <note>Referring to the "Mystical Authors" or writers on contemplative prayer.</note> make mention—

### Regarding the Letter on the Author of the Mystical [Works], Section 67.

...roughout; for instance, the author uses the word **exteriorly** <note>original: "exterius," used here to mean "outwardly" or "by heart"</note> in a peculiar way, as in: *If you knew the whole Bible exteriorly*. Likewise, in several places, instead of the word **easy** <note>original: "facilis"</note>, he uses the word **light** <note>original: "levis" or "leve"</note>, a term used by Germans and Belgians to signify something that is easy to do. Many other such instances will be easily noticed by a reader skilled in the German or Belgian languages.

Others have more probably noted that the fourth book, which is *On the Eucharist*, was not originally joined to the first three, nor did it belong to them. Instead, it constituted an entirely new and separate treatise, though by the same author. This opinion is supported by the old editions of **Thomas à Kempis's** works. 

Specifically, in the Paris folio edition of 1623, printed by **Badius Ascensius** <note>Josse Bade (1462–1535), a major printer in Paris; "Ascensius" refers to his birthplace of Asse, Belgium.</note> and titled *The Works of Thomas à Kempis, surnamed Malleolus* <note>original: "Malleolus," meaning "Little Hammer," the Latinized version of his family name, Hemerken.</note>, the first and second books are compressed into one, and the third follows under the name of the second. After every page has carried the title *The Imitation of Christ*, these words appear at the end, where the fourth book commonly begins: *Here begins the small book on the Sacraments*. Throughout all its pages, this section bears the title *On the Sacrament of the Altar*, and it concludes thus: *The book on the Sacrament of the Altar ends*, rather than *The Imitation of Christ*. Furthermore, in the *Contents* or the *Index* of the works, they list these as two separate items, just like two different treatises. A new edition of these works also appeared recently in Paris (1692)...

## Annotations & Additions

...[a] certain new <note>The Latin text begins with "va," likely completing "Nova" (New) from the preceding page.</note> French edition based on a very old copy written in Gothic script <note>Also known as "Blackletter," a script common in the Middle Ages.</note>, under the title ***Inner Consolation*** <note>original: *Consolatio interior*</note>. To this edition is prefixed a dissertation asserting that this specific copy also lacked the book regarding the Sacrament <note>Referring to Book 4 of the *Imitation*, "On the Holy Eucharist."</note>. Furthermore, it brings forth arguments not to be dismissed, asserting that the three books of the *Imitation* themselves were written not for Religious <note>Those bound by monastic vows.</note> or Monks, but for the conversion of the **Laity** and secular people. It argues that all those passages which in modern editions are restricted to Monks in various places, or written concerning things pertaining to them, are presented differently in that manuscript, being addressed to and written for all Christians. 

Therefore, those who more fiercely accuse the Protestants acted quite imprudently—specifically against the pious and learned **Castalio** <note>Sebastian Castellio (1515–1563), a theologian who edited the *Imitation* to be more universal, replacing monastic terms with general Christian ones.</note>, who had likewise applied such passages to all Christians and had also omitted the entire fourth book. They accused them as if they had thereby made themselves guilty of impiety and sacrilege.

### Regarding the Epistle on the Authors of the Mystics, Section 67.

...[Peters], the aim and character of which is the freedom of the soul in God and a tranquility that can be shaken or moved by no disturbances of worldly things, nor by any of their changes or accidents. This state is to be acquired through the renunciation of these very worldly things and of our own emotions, and through the elevation of the soul above all things into God and into His unique will, to which we hand over and resign ourselves entirely. This little book was published in Latin by the Abbot of the Canons of St. Genevieve in Paris, in 1659, with the title: ***The Other Thomas à Kempis, or the Ignited Soliloquy with God*** <note>original: *Ignitum cum Deo Soliloquium*</note> ***of the Reverend Lord Gerlach Peters of Deventer*** <note>original: *Daventriensis*</note>, etc. It was afterwards in the same place, in 1667, elegantly translated into the French language and released under the title, ***The Soliloquies of Gerlach—called another Thomas à Kempis***. Both editions placed the author's "Angelic Life" <note>A traditional term for a biography of a particularly holy or ascetic person.</note> at the beginning—the former more briefly, the latter at greater length. The same work had also appeared, translated from Latin into Dutch <note>original: *Belgicus*—in this context referring to the Dutch language of the Low Countries.</note>, in the year 1613 at 's-Hertogenbosch <note>original: *Sylvæducis*</note>. It is somewhat rare, although it deserves to be more common and very well known. 

Father **Joannes de Bonilla** <note>Juan de Bonilla (16th century), a Spanish Franciscan mystic known for his treatise on the peace of the soul.</note> uniquely belongs to this same character of peace and tranquility; he will also be discussed in the following article. **Hilarius Theomilus** <note>A pseudonym for a Pietist editor/translator, likely associated with Gottfried Arnold's circle.</note> recently translated him into German and included him in the second part of his excellent German book, (a) ***Continual Joy***.

*The Germanic Theology — this little book was written in German by a Teutonic Knight*,] Most people believe this booklet is called the GERMANIC Theology because it was originally written in the German language <note>original: "Germanico idiomate"</note>; this was also my own opinion. Since that Order is called the *Teutonic* Order <note>original: "Teutonicus"</note>, the book was named the TEUTONIC Theology from that source—that is, proceeding from an author of the Teutonic Order. Various editors later varied this title in different ways, and the Latin translator himself used the word "Germanic" <note>original: "Germanicam"</note> instead of the term "Teutonic," though with less precision. Furthermore, regarding the designation of the author's title or rank, all those are mistaken who, along with Neander <note>Michael Neander (1525–1595), a German teacher and philologist</note>, call him a *sacristan* <term>sacristan: original "aedituum," a lower-ranking official responsible for the physical upkeep of a church</term>, or even a "poor sacristan," because the ancient preface names him the *Custos* <term>Custos: a title meaning "Guardian" or "Warden," indicating a high-ranking administrative or spiritual supervisor</term> in the house of the Teutonic Knights at Frankfurt. Yet, a *Custos* is not the same as a sacristan; rather, it is a high rank among the primary members of many religious orders, and those who enjoy this rank are placed in charge of others...

...warding [these things], observing that they keep the laws and statutes of the Order; and also that its privileges are violated by none. Certainly the titles of *Teutonic Knight* <note>original: "Equitis Teutonici"</note> and *Priest* <note>original: "Presbyteri"</note>, which the same Preface assigns to this author, show clearly enough that he was by no means some poor sacristan <term>sacristan: original "aedituum," a lower-ranking official responsible for the physical upkeep of a church</term>, since they are titles of high dignity. Whether that house of Knights over which he presided was in Frankfurt am Main or Frankfurt an der Oder is a matter of doubt. I would believe it was the one on the Oder: for in those neighboring places that Order was powerful and held rule; and in those same places the first editions of the booklet appeared from the year 1518 onwards, among which one was issued at Königsberg <note>original: "Regiomonti"</note> in Prussia in the year 1558.

# Annotations & Additions

Theologians [have provided] annotations against Lucas Osiander <note>Lucas Osiander the Younger (1571–1638) was a prominent Lutheran polemicist who famously attacked Arndt for supposedly introducing mystical and "Catholic" errors into Lutheranism</note>, the quarrelsome Chancellor and Professor of Theology at the University of Tübingen. In order to defame and eliminate this divine book by Arndt, Osiander had frequently distorted and interpreted many passages in the worst possible light. Dorscheus <note>Johann Georg Dorsche (1597–1659), a Lutheran theologian who attempted to reconcile Arndt's work with orthodox dogma</note> wished to restore these passages to their proper meaning, but Arndt found more effective defenders of his work in Varenius, Breler, and others. You can find an account of his life in the work of the famous Arnold <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714), a radical Pietist historian</note> in the German treatise called *The Life of the Faithful* <note>original: "Vitæ fidelium" / "Das Leben der Gläubigen"</note>. I have also seen a *French* translation of Arndt's four books *On True Christianity* <note>original: "De Vero Christianismo"</note>, which was quite elegant, though not yet published; perhaps it will be released eventually, so that this excellent and beneficial work and book does not perish, which would be a cause for regret.

# Regarding the Epistle on the Authors of Mysticism, Sections 78 and 79.

### To Section 78, page 220, line 5.

*St. Clement in his divine Epistle translated into French by Mr. Te-serius]* <note>original: "D. Teserium"; likely referring to Balthasar de Tessereau, a 17th-century translator</note> That French translation of St. Clement’s Epistle to the Corinthians <note>An early Christian letter from the late 1st century, highly regarded by the early Church</note> suffers from many errors as well as omissions, perhaps through the fault of the typesetters. Mr. Arnold <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714), a German theologian and historian previously mentioned</note> translated the same better into German, together with the Epistle of Barnabas, and published it at Lüneburg in the year 1695. It is found, along with the Epistle of Polycarp (which is mentioned in the main text), among the writings or works of the Apostolic Fathers <note>A group of early Christian authors traditionally believed to have been disciples of the Apostles</note>, the former in Volume I and the latter in Volume II.

### To Section 79, page 221, line 8.

*A certain poor rustic, etc.]* His name was **JEAN DAUMONT** <note>original: "JOANNES DAUMONT"</note>, and he had been a vine-dresser, a labor which he afterwards gave up so that he might be more free for writing and the "cultivation" or spiritual direction of certain souls. Among his disciples were both the learned and preachers. He left behind very many writings, not yet published. He lived in Brittany <note>original: "Britannia Armorica"</note> and later in Paris. The things read in the tenth letter of Father Rigoleuc <note>Jean Rigoleuc (1595–1658), a Jesuit priest and prominent figure in the French school of spirituality</note> (in the volume of his shorter works, page 405) are to be understood as being about him, here translated into English from the Latin which was rendered from the original French: *Among those who are by their office entangled in the business (or labors) of the world, there are sometimes found souls so...*

### To the Epistle on the Mystical Authors, Section 79.

In that edition, there is that excellent work which is called *The Torrents* <note>original: "Torrentes"; published as "Les Torrents" in 1682, this is one of Guyon's most famous works, using the metaphor of streams returning to the ocean to describe the soul's journey back to God.</note>, because under the emblem and likeness of rushing torrents of water, it describes in a wonderful way many paths of purification. It is through these paths that those souls must pass who, in this life, ought to reach a state that is, as it were, Apostolic, so that they may then win others for God. Many traces of this state are presented here and there in the following *Explication of the Song of Songs* <note>original: "Explicatione Cantici Canticorum"</note> by the same author. Added to these small works is a short treatise found later (a) titled *Rules for those who have devoted themselves to honoring and imitating the Infancy of Jesus Christ* <note>original: "Regularum pro illis qui Infantiae Jesu Christi"</note>, and who have for that purpose established a certain society among themselves. That noble Lady <note>Madame Guyon.</note> is said to be still among the living, and indeed free, living in retirement at the home of her son-in-law, the Count of V... <note>Louis-Nicolas de la Motte, Count de Vaux.</note> in the province of Gâtinais <note>original: "Vastiniensi"; a historical region in north-central France.</note>. Also presented later was the booklet of her Director, *Father François de la Combe, A Brief Instruction on Christian Perfection* <note>original: "P.F. de la Combe, Brevis instructio ad Perfectionem Christianam"; La Combe was Guyon's spiritual guide and was imprisoned for many years due to his association with her teachings.</note> etc., which was afterwards printed separately.

It should be noted that the first words of the *Treatise of the Torrents* <note>original: "Tractatus Torrentium"</note> were initially subject to ambiguity. In the manuscript, there were, first, the names *Jesus, Mary, Joseph*. Then followed the title, *The Beginning* <note>original: "Exordium"</note>

---

### To the Epistle on the Mystical Authors, Section 85.

->To Section 85, page 233, line 3.<-

**Behold, therefore, the true character of those same (writings of the Virgin Antoinette Bourignon), etc.]** This "character" or nature can be expressed according to their goal in the following way. These writings, namely, aim toward this: that when—through the practice of the Gospel doctrine contained therein and through the surrender of our will into the hands of the Lord, upon whom we wish to depend entirely—we are prepared as a dwelling for the Holy Spirit; He himself may then be able to come to us, and henceforth dwell in us, and there resume His lordship <note>The author emphasizes the "interior kingdom," a central theme in 17th-century mysticism where God rules directly within the soul.</note>. He comes intending to enrich us with His wisdom and the treasures of the riches of Christ, to enlighten, animate, and teach us, and thereafter to direct all things, having been thoroughly restored according to His divine will. He would have done this indeed (not to say even more excellently) if the Fall of Adam <note>original: "lapsus Adami"; the theological concept that humanity lost its original state of perfection and direct communion with God through the first sin.</note> had not intervened and acted as an obstacle. Truly, it is evident in itself that nothing in this life can be more sublime or more perfect for a Christian than this state. Consequently, those who repeatedly claim that these writings can only serve beginners testify by this very fact that they have not read them at all, and speak only from the envious reports of others; they are entirely unaware whether what they themselves say is even relevant. It is far otherwise for anyone who wishes to consider this matter in the proper way and spirit, as is evident from even one <note>The text cuts off here, likely continuing the argument on the following page.</note>

By the recent testimony of a certain anonymous person, describing the CHARACTER <note>original: "CHARACTEREM"; referring to the essential nature or spiritual quality of the works.</note> of those books—known to him through experience—in (a) his own book, very recently published under my care, in this way:

*The divine writings of the Virgin Antoinette Bourignon <note>Antoinette Bourignon (1616–1680) was a Flemish mystic who claimed direct revelation and critiqued the organized churches of her time.</note>, whatever those blinded by the prejudices of their own Sect may say, or those who—not without a haughty brow—despise everything proposed by a woman, contain such a treasure of divine light within them that whoever wishes to do the will of Him who sent Christ of old, and now His faithful servant—not to say Bride <note>The "Bride of Christ" is a common mystical term for a soul or person in a state of perfect spiritual union with God.</note>—will very easily come to know whether the doctrine is from God, or whether she spoke and wrote of her own accord. Whoever reads those writings with this sincere intention—namely, of actually carrying out the known will of God—and likewise with a free and tranquil mind, I promise him, and I promise confidently and sincerely before the face of the Lord, that he will confess with me that nothing can be said either more expressively, or more clearly, or more extensively, or more powerfully, or what represents the present state of Christianity <note>original: "Christianiſmi"</note> more truly and vividly; or what so lucidly separates good from evil, truth from falsehood, the essential from the accessory in all Sects; or [what better exposes] the Devil's great power over the children of unbelief and over the elements of this world, and even the most cunning snares he lays for men of good will—*

### To the Epistle concerning the Authors of Mysteries § 89.

It is shameful to even point out such filth. I will only say that he <note>Referring to Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), the "Censor" whose *Historical and Critical Dictionary* entry on Bourignon was highly skeptical and often mocking.</note> did not even correctly express the mind of the one he wished to harass; and such a Censor is to be blamed for the ignorance with which he marked as a "very singular aberration of mind" in ***Antonia B.*** her opinion regarding Adam having—not "limbs" (as he obscenely jokes)—but the internal principles of both sexes. 

This opinion, however, is held by both the ancient Hebrews and Kabbalists <term>Kabbalists: Practitioners of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah), which often describes the first human, Adam Kadmon, as containing both male and female divine energies.</term>, and by as many modern philosophers as have scrutinized the more abstruse parts of nature. It is held specifically by almost everyone I mentioned in the entire section on ***Jacob Boehme*** <note>Jacob Boehme (1575–1624) was a German mystic who proposed that the original Adam was an androgynous being who did not reproduce through sexual organs.</note>, and even by this Boehme himself and all his followers. 

Furthermore, our author <note>Bayle</note> poorly equates the earth to a woman; for while a woman contributes one of the seminal principles to the act of generation <term>Seminal principles: In pre-modern biology, these were the "seeds" or vital forces believed to be contained in reproductive matter that directed the growth of an organism.</term>, the earth does not do so in the same way. Nor indeed does a plant depend on a place in the earth for the propagation of its likeness in such an imperfect and unhappy way as a man depends on a woman—who not infrequently stands in the way of his liberty and happiness, as was seen even in the case of Adam. 

In another place, this same man picks at an innocent expression in which childbirth is alluded to by even a single word, though he himself has most foully defiled six hundred pages with obscenities <note>original: *obscœnitatibus*; a reference to the many controversial and sexually explicit footnotes in Bayle’s *Dictionary*.</note> unworthy of an honest man.

However, from writings and legal documents <note>original: "instrumentisque"</note> discovered later, the matter must be corrected in this way: several years before, while she was still entirely free in that regard, she had already donated those properties of her own accord and by an authentic legal deed to the Lille Hospital. However, she had wished this donation to remain hidden between herself and the directors of the Hospital for as long as she lived. Yet, on the occasion of that persecution discussed there, she had to permit the directors to make the donation public then, to prevent the plundering of those goods, since it was then clear that those properties had long belonged to the poor by her authentic gift.

# FAITH AND REASON
# COMPARED,
## And each restored to its proper place,
### *against the Principles*
# OF JOHN LOCKE. <note>John Locke (1632–1704) was a hugely influential English philosopher. His "Essay Concerning Human Understanding" (1689) discussed how much we can know through reason versus faith, which sparked intense debate among theologians like Poiret.</note>

->Including many things by which the<-
->**more worthy chapters of DIVINE REVELATION and the**<-

### With a TRIPLE SUPPLEMENT
->1. On implicit, or bare, Faith.<-
->2. On the Certainty and meaning of the Holy Scriptures.<-
->3. On Perfection and Happiness in this life.<-

->*Edited and with a preface by*<-
## PIERRE POIRET. <note>Pierre Poiret (1646–1719) was a French mystical philosopher and theologian. Originally a follower of Descartes, he later became a leader in the mystical movement, publishing the works of famous mystics like Madame Guyon.</note>

### AMSTERDAM,
## From the WETSTEIN Press. <note>original: "Ex Officina WETSTENIANA"; the Wetstein family were famous printers and booksellers in Amsterdam, known for high-quality academic and religious texts.</note>
->1708.<- <note>original: "cIɔ Iɔ cc VIII." This is an archaic way of writing Roman numerals. The symbol cIɔ represents 1,000, and Iɔ represents 500. Therefore, 1000 + 500 + 200 + 8 = 1708.</note>

<summary>The title page for Pierre Poiret's "Faith and Reason Compared," a work defending mystical Christianity against the rationalism of John Locke. It highlights supplements on the nature of faith, the certainty of the Bible, and spiritual happiness.</summary>
